did_you_know.text: Did you know? On the first day of the seventh month, there was a sacred assembly, no ordinary work was permitted, and it is called in the Torah “a day of trumpet blasts.”
Did you know? The additional offering for the day of trumpet blasts consisted of one young bull, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old, all without blemish.
Did you know? The offerings for the day of trumpet blasts were presented in addition to the monthly burnt offering, the regular daily burnt offering, and their grain offerings and drink offerings.
Did you know? On the tenth day of the seventh month, there was a sacred assembly, and the Israelites were commanded to afflict themselves and do no work.

Did you know? The offering for the Day of Atonement is described as being presented in addition to the sin offering of atonement, the regular daily burnt offering, and its grain offering and drink offering.
Did you know? The Festival of Booths begins on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and lasts seven days as a festival to the Lord.
Did you know? On the first day of the Festival of Booths, thirteen bulls, two rams, and fourteen male lambs, all without blemish, were offered, in addition to a male goat as a sin offering.

Did you know? During the Festival of Booths, the number of bulls offered each day decreases: thirteen on the first day, twelve on the second, and down to seven on the seventh day. In contrast, the number of rams and lambs remains constant—two rams and fourteen lambs each day.

Did you know? The eighth day of the Festival of Booths is called “the solemn assembly” in the Torah. On that day, one bull, one ram, and seven lambs were offered, in addition to a male goat as a sin offering.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, it is stated that the offerings for the appointed festivals are in addition to vows, freewill offerings, burnt offerings, grain offerings, drink offerings, and fellowship offerings—in other words, they do not replace these personal offerings.
